topics.title: Differential & Integral Calculus (Power Rule, Chain Rule & Area)
topics.summary: First principles, derivatives dy/dx, stationary points, tangents/normals, and definite integrals.
sourceNotes: The derivative dy/dx gives the instantaneous gradient of the tangent to the curve y = f(x) at any point.
At a stationary point, dy/dx = 0. If d²y/dx² > 0, it is a local minimum; if d²y/dx² < 0, it is a local maximum.
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the definite integral ∫[a to b] f(x) dx equals F(b) - F(a) and represents signed area under the curve.
topics.workedExample: Find stationary points of y = x³ - 6x² + 9x + 1: dy/dx = 3x² - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0 -> x = 1, 3. At x = 1, d²y/dx² = 6(1) - 12 = -6 < 0 (Max); at x = 3, d²y/dx² = +6 > 0 (Min).
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting the constant of integration '+ C' in indefinite integrals or forgetting the inner derivative when applying the Chain Rule.
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Pure Mathematics & Calculus (9709)
learningObjectives: First principles, derivatives dy/dx, stationary points, tangents/normals, and definite integrals.

topics.title: Arithmetic/Geometric Series, Binomial Expansion & Circular Measure
topics.summary: AP and GP nth term and sum formulas, sum to infinity S_∞ = a/(1 - r), radians, and (a + b)ⁿ.
keyFormulas: Arc Length: s = rθ, Sector Area: A = ½r²θ (θ in radians)
sourceNotes: An infinite geometric progression converges to a finite sum S_∞ = a/(1 - r) if and only if the common ratio satisfies |r| < 1.
Arc length s = rθ and sector area A = ½r²θ are valid ONLY when angle θ is measured in radians (π rad = 180°).
topics.workedExample: Find the sum to infinity of 18 + 6 + 2 + ...: First term a = 18, common ratio r = 6/18 = 1/3 (|r| < 1). S_∞ = 18 / (1 - 1/3) = 18 / (2/3) = 27.
topics.commonMisconception: Using degrees instead of radians in s = rθ or applying S_∞ = a/(1 - r) when |r| ≥ 1.
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Pure Mathematics & Calculus (9709)
learningObjectives: AP and GP nth term and sum formulas, sum to infinity S_∞ = a/(1 - r), radians, and (a + b)ⁿ.

topics.title: 2D Projectile Motion, Linear Momentum & Wave Superposition
topics.summary: Independence of horizontal/vertical motion, elastic vs. inelastic collisions, stationary waves, and double-slit interference.
keyFormulas: Elastic Collision: Relative speed of approach = Relative speed of separation
Young's Double Slit: λ = ax / D
sourceNotes: Total linear momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (both elastic and inelastic) provided no external resultant force acts on the system.
Kinetic energy is conserved ONLY in perfectly elastic collisions.
In projectile motion (ignoring air drag), horizontal velocity v_x = u cos θ remains constant while vertical motion has constant downward acceleration g.
topics.workedExample: A 2 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides and sticks to a stationary 2 kg trolley. By conservation of momentum: (2)(4) + 0 = (2 + 2)v -> v = 2 m/s.
topics.commonMisconception: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision just because momentum is conserved.
learningObjectives: Independence of horizontal/vertical motion, elastic vs. inelastic collisions, stationary waves, and double-slit interference.

topics.title: Hess's Law, Chemical Equilibrium (Le Chatelier) & Organic Mechanisms
topics.summary: Enthalpy cycles, Kc and Kp expressions, Le Chatelier's principle, and nucleophilic/electrophilic mechanisms.
sourceNotes: Hess's Law states that the total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is independent of the pathway taken, provided initial and final conditions are identical.
Only temperature changes the numerical value of the equilibrium constant Kc; catalysts speed up both forward and reverse rates equally without shifting equilibrium position.
topics.workedExample: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (ΔH = -92 kJ/mol, exothermic): Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the right (fewer gas moles: 2 vs 4); increasing temperature shifts it left.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking adding a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of products or alters Kc.
learningObjectives: Enthalpy cycles, Kc and Kp expressions, Le Chatelier's principle, and nucleophilic/electrophilic mechanisms.

topics.title: Cell Structure, Protein Synthesis & Enzyme Kinetics (Km & Vmax)
topics.summary: Ultrastructure of eukaryotic organelles, transcription, translation (ribosomal codons), and Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics.
learningObjectives: Explain the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure and calculate actual sizes using magnification formulas
Describe transcription and translation, and determine Michaelis-Menten constant (Km) from Lineweaver-Burk plots
keyFormulas: Magnification Formula: M = I / A (Magnification = Image Size / Actual Size)
Michaelis-Menten: Lower Km indicates higher enzyme affinity for the substrate
Non-competitive Inhibition: Vmax decreases, Km remains unchanged; Competitive Inhibition: Vmax unchanged, Km increases
sourceNotes: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) provides high resolution for organelle ultrastructure; scanning electron microscopy (SEM) yields 3D surface topographies.
Enzymes lower the activation energy barrier without altering the overall free energy change (ΔG) of the reaction.
Transfer RNA (tRNA) anticodons bind antiparallel to messenger RNA (mRNA) codons on the ribosome.
topics.workedExample: An organelle measures 12 mm on a micrograph with magnification ×20,000. Calculate actual diameter in micrometers: A = I / M = 12 mm / 20,000 = 0.0006 mm = 0.6 μm.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to convert image measurement units (mm) into micrometers (μm) before dividing by magnification.

topics.title: Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists, Binary Trees & Recursion
topics.summary: Dynamic data structures (pointers, nodes), LIFO vs. FIFO queues, binary search tree traversal (in-order, pre-order, post-order), and call stack recursion.
learningObjectives: Write algorithms to implement operations on linear abstract data types: stacks, queues, and singly linked lists
Trace and write recursive subroutines, evaluating the call stack overhead and base case termination
keyFormulas: Binary Search Tree In-Order Traversal: Left Subtree -> Root -> Right Subtree (yields sorted output)
Stack (LIFO): push(x), pop(), peek() in O(1) time complexity
Queue (FIFO): enqueue(x) at tail, dequeue() from head
sourceNotes: Dynamic data structures grow and shrink at runtime in heap memory, avoiding fixed array size limits.
A recursive algorithm must have at least one base case that returns without recursion, preventing stack overflow errors.
Linked list deletion involves updating the previous node's next pointer to bypass the target node.
topics.workedExample: Recursive Factorial: fact(3) -> 3 * fact(2) -> 3 * (2 * fact(1)) -> 3 * (2 * 1) = 6. Call stack pushes stack frames for each call until base case n <= 1 is met, then unwinds.
topics.commonMisconception: Omitting the base case in recursive functions, causing an infinite recursion and a StackOverflowException.

subjects.subjectName: Advanced Calculus, Differential Equations & Complex Numbers

topics.title: Integration by Parts, Partial Fractions, Differential Equations & Argand Diagrams
topics.summary: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, separable first-order ODEs, and complex numbers z = x + iy = r·e^(iθ).
keyFormulas: Integration by Parts: ∫ u (dv/dx) dx = u·v - ∫ v (du/dx) dx
Euler's Form: r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r·e^(iθ)
sourceNotes: To solve a separable differential equation dy/dx = f(x)g(y), separate variables onto respective sides, integrate both sides, and use initial conditions to determine the constant.
On an Argand diagram, multiplying a complex number by r·e^(iθ) scales its modulus by r and rotates its argument anticlockwise by angle θ.
topics.workedExample: Solve dy/dx = 2xy given y(0) = 3: Separate -> ∫ (1/y) dy = ∫ 2x dx -> ln|y| = x² + C -> y = A·e^(x²). Since y(0) = 3, A = 3 -> y = 3e^(x²).
topics.commonMisconception: Adding the constant +C after exponentiating as y = e^(x²) + C instead of multiplying as y = A·e^(x²).
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Advanced Calculus, Differential Equations & Complex Numbers
learningObjectives: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, separable first-order ODEs, and complex numbers z = x + iy = r·e^(iθ).

topics.title: Photoelectric Effect, Faraday's Induction & Mass-Energy Equivalence
topics.summary: Photon energy E = hf, work function Φ, de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, magnetic flux linkage, and ΔE = Δmc².
keyFormulas: de Broglie: λ = h / p = h / (mv)
sourceNotes: The photoelectric effect demonstrates the particle nature of light: each photon interacts one-to-one with a single electron. Below threshold frequency f₀, no photoelectrons are emitted regardless of intensity.
Above threshold frequency, increasing light intensity increases the number of emitted electrons per second (photocurrent) but does NOT increase their maximum kinetic energy.
topics.workedExample: Light of photon energy 4.2 eV strikes a metal with work function Φ = 2.5 eV. Maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons KE_max = 4.2 - 2.5 = 1.7 eV.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking brighter light (higher intensity) increases the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons.
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Quantum Physics, Electromagnetism & Nuclear Physics
learningObjectives: Photon energy E = hf, work function Φ, de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, magnetic flux linkage, and ΔE = Δmc².

topics.title: Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra / A*), Big-O Complexity & Neural Networks
topics.summary: Shortest-path heuristics, recursion & dynamic programming, backpropagation, and transformer attention basics.
keyFormulas: A* Cost Function: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
sourceNotes: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights; A* adds an admissible heuristic h(n) to guide search toward the goal.
Neural networks learn by computing a loss function L on predictions and updating weights in the opposite direction of the gradient via backpropagation.
topics.workedExample: In A* search, if node B has actual path cost from start g(B) = 6 and estimated heuristic distance to goal h(B) = 4, its priority score is f(B) = 6 + 4 = 10.
topics.commonMisconception: Using an inadmissible heuristic h(n) that overestimates true distance, which can cause A* to miss the optimal shortest path.
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Computer Science, Algorithms & Artificial Intelligence
learningObjectives: Shortest-path heuristics, recursion & dynamic programming, backpropagation, and transformer attention basics.

topics.title: Aggregate Demand/Supply (AD-AS), Fiscal Multipliers & Central Banking
topics.summary: GDP components (C + I + G + (X - M)), Keynesian multiplier, inflation vs. unemployment, and interest rates.
keyFormulas: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / Price Index
sourceNotes: Aggregate Demand (AD) is the total spending on domestically produced goods and services: Consumption (C) + Investment (I) + Government Spending (G) + Net Exports (X - M).
When a central bank raises interest rates (contractionary monetary policy), borrowing becomes more expensive, cooling investment and consumption to curb demand-pull inflation.
topics.workedExample: If the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.8, the spending multiplier is k = 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5. A $10B government infrastructure injection can expand equilibrium GDP by up to $50B.
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing Nominal GDP growth (which includes price inflation) with Real GDP growth (which measures actual output volume).
topics.syllabusCode: Cambridge International A-Level Macroeconomics, Monetary Policy & Global Trade
learningObjectives: GDP components (C + I + G + (X - M)), Keynesian multiplier, inflation vs. unemployment, and interest rates.
